title: Superconductivity in High-Entropy Alloy System Containing Tb.

recollection.starting_material: Probably an equiatomic high-entropy alloy made by arc-melting several refractory or rare-earth metals together with terbium, e.g. (Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti–Tb) or a similar multi-principal-element mix.
recollection.intervention: Likely prepared by repeated arc-melting (or induction melting) under argon, followed by homogenizing anneal and possibly cold-rolling and re-annealing; superconducting properties measured by four-probe resistivity and magnetization down to a few kelvin.
recollection.structure: Most high-entropy superconductors crystallize in a single-phase body-centered cubic solid solution, so the alloy probably formed a BCC lattice with random occupation of lattice sites by the constituent elements including Tb.
recollection.mechanism: Conventional phonon-mediated BCS superconductivity arising from strong electron-phonon coupling in the disordered BCC lattice; the role of Tb would be to tune the density of states and possibly add magnetic scattering that suppresses Tc at higher concentrations.
recollection.results: My guess is that the alloy showed bulk superconductivity with an onset critical temperature around 2–4 K, an upper critical field μ0Hc2(0) of roughly 1–3 T, and a relatively large Sommerfeld coefficient indicating enhanced electronic density of states. Adding more Tb probably lowered Tc, consistent with magnetic pair-breaking.

score.note: The recollection generically identifies arc-melting under argon and a refractory BCC alloy, but invents annealing/rolling and misses the direct Tb-free versus Tb-containing comparison. It correctly anticipates a BCC matrix and possible superconductivity suppression from Tb, yet incorrectly assumes a single phase and omits Tb/Tb2O3 precipitates, their reduction of superconducting volume, and the paper's inconclusive attribution of the degradation. The estimated Tc (2–4 K) and Hc2 (1–3 T) are substantially below the actual 4.6 K and 6.1 T.
